Neonatal chicken turtles (Deirochelys reticularia) emerge from parchment-shelled eggs with a carapace length of approximately 3 centimeters [Lb = approximately 3 centimeters]. These hatchlings typically weigh about 11 grams [Wwb = about 11 grams] at emergence, though geographic variation in maternal investment can yield individuals ranging from 8.7 to 13.3 grams. The plastron length at birth, a standard measure in chelonian morphometrics, spans from 22.3 to 32.7 millimeters. Incubation duration is strongly temperature-dependent; eggs maintained at a constant 27 °C [T = 27 °C] require roughly 159 days [ab = roughly 159 days] to complete development and initiate hatching. This relatively protracted incubation period aligns with observations from South Carolina, where nests at 29 °C averaged 152 days until emergence, while Florida populations at similar temperatures achieve eclosion in as little as 78 to 89 days. The yolk-dependent embryo absorbs substantial lipid reserves during this extended incubation, which likely sustains the lecithotrophic larva through the yolk-sac resorption phase before the onset of exogenous feeding.

Sexual maturation in Deirochelys reticularia proceeds along markedly different trajectories between males and females. Under typical thermal conditions of 22 °C [T = 22 °C], males attain puberty at approximately 2.3 years after hatching [tp = approximately 2.3 years after hatching], corresponding to about 840 days post-emergence. Females require considerably more time, reaching sexual maturity at roughly 5 years after hatching [tp = roughly 5 years after hatching] under the same thermal regime at a temperature of 22 °C [T = 22 °C]. This pronounced sexual dimorphism in maturation timing is reflected in body size at puberty: males become reproductively active once their carapace length reaches about 10.2 centimeters [Lp = about 10.2 centimeters], whereas females delay first reproduction until their carapace measures approximately 17.8 centimeters [Lp = approximately 17.8 centimeters]. The divergence in size at puberty corresponds to a broader pattern of female-biased sexual size dimorphism across the species. Gravid females, upon reaching reproductive activation, produce clutches that range from 1 to 10 eggs per clutch [N_R_i = 1 to 10 eggs per clutch], with most individuals depositing one, and occasionally two, clutches annually [F_R_i = one, and occasionally two, clutches annually] when maintained at 22 °C [T = 22 °C].

Ultimate body size in chicken turtles exhibits pronounced sexual dimorphism, consistent with patterns observed across many emydid species. Females attain a maximum carapace length of 25.4 centimeters [Li = 25.4 centimeters], while males reach a substantially smaller ultimate carapace length of approximately 15 centimeters [Li = approximately 15 centimeters]. This female-biased size disparity, where females are roughly 1.5 times larger than males, likely reflects selective pressures favoring increased fecundity through greater abdominal volume for egg production. The ultimate wet weight recorded for large adult females approaches 2763 grams [Wwi = 2763 grams], a mass comparable to that reported for Graptemys ouachitensis, a similarly sized emydid turtle. This asymptotic mass is achieved only after several years of sustained growth following the juvenile phase. Young-of-year individuals, by contrast, exhibit rapid linear growth during their first growing season, doubling their birth carapace length within the initial months of exogenous feeding.

Longevity records for Deirochelys reticularia indicate a maximum lifespan of approximately 8760 days [am = approximately 8760 days] when individuals are maintained under consistently favorable conditions at 22 °C [T = 22 °C]. This relatively extended lifespan, exceeding that of many smaller emydids, reflects a life-history strategy characterized by delayed maturity, iteroparity, and sustained reproductive output across multiple decades. Field studies using mark-recapture methods have documented individuals persisting well into their second decade, with senescence-related mortality rates increasing only after approximately 20 years of age. The species' ability to achieve such longevity is closely tied to its conservative metabolic strategy; as ectotherms, chicken turtles allocate minimal energy to meeting their daily energetic costs compared to endothermic vertebrates of equivalent body mass. This energetic efficiency allows reproductively active adults to divert substantial resources toward egg production across numerous breeding seasons, even as their bodily growth slows following the attainment of ultimate body size.

The ecological niche of Deirochelys reticularia is intimately linked to ephemeral wetland habitats across the southeastern United States, where seasonal hydroperiods shape foraging opportunities and predator exposure. Juvenile chicken turtles occupy shallow, densely vegetated margins of temporary ponds, where they exploit abundant invertebrate prey during the active feeding onset phase. As individuals transition from the lecithotrophic larval stage to exogenous feeding, they exhibit a pronounced trophic switch toward greater carnivory, consuming crayfish, aquatic insects, and amphibian larvae. This dietary flexibility likely contributes to the species' broad geographic distribution, which spans coastal plains from Virginia to Texas. Comparative studies with syntopic emydids such as Pseudemys floridana reveal that Deirochelys reticularia achieves higher population densities in habitats with prolonged hydroperiods, presumably because extended aquatic residency reduces terrestrial predation risk and increases foraging time for growing juveniles. The species' reliance on temporary wetlands, however, renders it vulnerable to habitat alteration from drainage and agricultural conversion across much of its range.
